slides.title: Direct Sign-In lifecycle
slides.subtitle: Take the callback once, exchange the code, upgrade the same Session
slides.notes: This example picks up where the boundary example stopped: the user has approved on the company's page. The host now has to turn the browser callback into a signed-in Session, once, and without widening access.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.statement: Sign-in upgrades **the same Session**. Partial consent is a **result**, not an error.
slides.notes: The user is signed in on the Session the conversation already has, not a new one. And if the user grants less than was asked, the host reports it plainly instead of quietly asking for more.

slides.title: Who takes part

columns.heading: User and browser
columns.content: Approves `orders:read`, declines `orders:return`; the browser hits the registered HTTPS callback.

columns.heading: PAP host
columns.content: Takes the pending state from **Reactor**, verifies, and exchanges the code.

columns.heading: Company
columns.content: Issues the signed-in DPoP token, after one **nonce** challenge.

slides.notes: The user approves one scope and declines the other. The company redirects the browser to the host's registered callback. The host uses the Reactor state store, a signer and a DPoP provider to finish the exchange.

slides.title: From callback to checks

items.title: Callback
items.detail: Code, state and issuer reach the host

slides.notes: The callback carries a code, the state and the issuer. The host takes the pending request out of the store in one atomic step, getting back the verifier and the existing session_id, then checks the redirect, state, issuer and expiry.

slides.title: The exchange

items.title: Retry once
items.detail: Same code and verifier, fresh assertion and proof

slides.notes: The host exchanges the code with a client assertion and a DPoP proof. The company asks for a nonce, so the host retries once: same authorization code and verifier, but a fresh assertion and a fresh proof. The answer is a signed-in token for the same Session, with orders:read.

slides.title: What gets validated
items: Redirect location, issuer, state and expiry
Content type, response size and token type
Sign-in status and the **same** Session ID
Scopes: never more than requested; missing ones reported
slides.notes: Everything the company sends back is checked. If the company returns a scope the user was never asked for, the host rejects it. Scopes that are missing are reported, so the application can degrade or explain.

slides.title: A replayed callback
slides.statement: State is consumed **before** the exchange. The second callback finds **nothing** and is rejected.
slides.notes: The example submits the callback twice. Because the state was taken out of the store before the exchange, whether it then failed or succeeded, the second attempt finds no state and is rejected.

slides.title: What stays where

right.heading: What the user and model see

slides.notes: The Account Token goes into the host's token store before complete returns; the result carries only a reference, with no refresh token. No token reaches URLs, logs, analytics, React state or a model transcript.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples grant only orders:read, then replay the callback
slides.notes: Both examples ask for read and return access, get read only, and show the replayed callback being rejected. The Direct Sign-In guide covers the production setup.
